titleStmt.title: An EVT-based Worst-Case Response Time Analysis of Complex Real-Time Systems

analytic.title: An EVT-based Worst-Case Response Time Analysis of Complex Real-Time Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: In recent years, the complexity of real-time embedded systems has increased dramatically. For those modern real-time systems, the limitations of original static Response Time Analysis (RTA) become more and more conspicuous. Most static analysis methods not only require much detailed system information, but also only target to some specific system model with non-realistic assumptions. As a result, those methods may produce overly pessimistic results, making them unsuitable to be applied on a complex industrial system. The best system model may be the system itself. Therefore, statistical RTA, which can produce probabilistic analysis results based on samples provided by real systems or simulators, may become more expedient. Statistical RTA usually requires more relaxed assumptions and less system information than static RTA. In this paper, we present an Extreme Value Theory (EVT) based method to compute Worst-Case Response Time (WCRT) targeting complex realtime systems. In the evaluation phase, we have applied this method to the calculation of worst-case transmission delays of messages over Controller Area Network (CAN), and some comparisons with static RTA are also provided. According to the experimental results, as the system complexity increases, our approach performs much more stable and less pessimistic.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The predictability of timing behavior is very important for real-time embedded systems. The research on timing analysis of real-time systems can be traced back to several decades ago. Most existing analysis methods are based on deterministic Response Time Analysis (RTA) [1]. In [2], Joseph et al. first derived the exact response time analysis of preemptive realtime systems with fixed priorities. The analysis was later extended by Burns et al. [3] and Audsley el al. [4] to support non-preemptive behavior and release jitter. In [5], Tindell et al. applied the static RTA on the timing analysis of Controller Area Network (CAN) communication, which was later revised by Davis et al. in [6]. In order to generate more applicable analysis, many other methods have been proposed which take additional factors into account, such as task offsets [7] [8], task dependencies [9], and mixed task models [10]. Even though many factors have been considered, it is still very difficult to analyze a real industrial system using those methods. One important reason is that there is usually some unpredictable randomness in a real system which cannot be accurately modeled. Moreover, those methods always require much detailed system information, such as task Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET). As far as we know, there is still no approved method to compute extremely tight WCET. In order to provide guaranteed results, those methods have to include varying degrees of pessimism as a price. As a result, for a complex real-time system, those static analysis may generate overly pessimistic results, or they may even be unapplicable.

As we know, guaranteed upper bounds of WCRT are very important for hard real-time systems. However, a lot of systems may not have strictly hard real-time requirements. These systems, known as soft real-time systems, can afford some timing constraint violations up to some level, using appropriate mechanisms which may be similar to some fault tolerant solutions. If such systems are designed based on some overly pessimistic analysis results provided by some static RTA, the waste of resource can be very high. Moreover, WCRT may not be interesting for soft real-time systems. Instead, some applications depend more on the average timing performance, such as Automatic Cruise Control and Automated Parking [11]. Therefore, many researchers have tried to develop different approaches to achieve probabilistic RTA, which may provide either an upper bound of WCRT with some probability, or a probability distribution of response times with a confidence level. In [12], Manolache et al. have proposed a stochastic schedulability analysis assuming a generalized probability distribution (Coxian distribution of exponentials) of execution times. Diaz et al. have presented a stochastic response time analysis method for periodic real-time systems in [13]. The method can be applied on both static and dynamic priority scheduling, and can support arbitrary deadlines as well as varying execution time distributions. Some stochastic analysis methods have also been developed for CAN networks, such as the approach in [14] which takes a probability distribution of bit-stuffing into account, and the method in [15] which provides a probabilistic analysis of transmission latencies considering task response times as well as sampling delays. Most of these methods still depend on much detailed system information and maybe unrealistic assumptions. Therefore, some researchers came up with another type of analysis using statistical tools.

In [11], Haibo et al. have presented a statistical method to predict the distribution of message response times in CAN. The analysis, using a mixed model of the Gamma distribution and the Degenerate distribution, can achieve a good performance even when only partial system information is available. In [16] and [17], the authors discussed the statistical analysis 978-1-4799-0658-1/13/$31.00 c 2013 IEEE 8th IEEE International Symposium on Industrial Embedded Systems (SIES 2013) of WCET using Extreme Value Theory (EVT) which is usually used to analyze rarely occurred scenarios of an event. The Gumbel Max distribution is selected to fit the analyzed samples, since it is usually used to model the maximum extreme cases [18], which adapts the concept of WCET. Lu et al. extend these works and apply the analysis on WCRT in [19], where a systematic analysis framework is provided. These EVT based approaches do not require any detailed knowledge of the task sets, and can be generally applied on different system models. However, the approach presented in [19] may not be applicable for some cases. For example, after the maxima selection phase, the remained samples are quite possible to fail to match the Gumbel Max distribution in some cases. As a result, the number of recalculation times may increase. Moreover, one parameters is not selected appropriately in that work, which is the acceptance probability used in the Gumbel Max percent point function making the conclusion of results (i.e. probability of response time violation) incorrect.

In this paper, we present an improved EVT based WCRT analysis method which is extended from some previous works. This approach can be generally applied on different system models, since the system under analysis is considered as a black box. We have evaluated our approach using two different case studies of message transmissions over a CAN bus. Comparisons between our solution and static RTA are also presented.

In Section II, we briefly describe some basic knowledge of the statistical tools used in our method. Section III illustrates the details of our approach, and two case studies with some discussions of the observations are provided in Section IV. Finally, Section V concludes the paper along with some future work.

div.head: A. Extreme Value Theory
div.p: Traditionally, most statistical tools focus on the means of data sets. However, for some problems, the extreme events are more relevant, such as the probabilities of the arrival of a catastrophic storm, the occurrence of an earthquake as well as the appearance of a WCRT in a complex real-time system. Extreme Value Theory (EVT) is a branch of the statistical family, which is always used to handle extreme scenarios for some events as the above examples. In other words, EVT is used to analyze the tails of a probability distribution of a sequence of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) random variables.

EVT involves two types of analysis methods: Block Maxima and Peak Over Threshold (POT). In the former approach, the data set is divided into same sized blocks, and the set of maxima which is used for further analysis, consists of the maximum value of each block. In the latter method, the analysis is based on the excesses of samples over a selected high threshold.

Assume that a data set X i = {X 1 , X 2 ,...,X n } consists of independent random variables with the same distribution. According to EVT, if M i = max(X 1 ,...,X n ), the distribution of the new data set M formed by M i will converge to the Generalized Extreme Value (GEV) distribution as n goes to infinite [20]. GEV distribution provides a probability law of the Block Maxima approach, and is a combination of three standard Extreme Value distribution functions depending on the shape parameter ξ:

• if ξ > 0: Fréchet distribution (Type II): which has a bounded lower side and a heavy upper tail (maxima related); • if ξ = 0: Gumbel distribution (Type I): which is unbounded and has a non-heavy upper tail; • if ξ < 0: Weibull distribution (Type III): which has a finite upper endpoint (minima related).

Assume that a data set X = {X 1 , X 2 ,...,X n } is formed by a sequence of independent identically distributed random variables, and u is a selected high threshold. According to EVT, the probability distribution of the new data set Y , which is formed by the exceedances Y i = X iu, will converge to the Generalized Pareto Distribution (GPD). This is the theoretical base of the POT analysis approach. The shape parameters of GPD and GEV are identical, and their scale parameters are related [20].

Block Maxima and POT are both widely applied in different areas. The former method is usually easier to apply, but the estimation uncertainties may be large depending on the sample size. If the threshold is selected appropriately, POT can perform more efficient (i.e. a lower threshold may result in more available exceedances). However, the threshold must be selected very carefully. If the threshold is too low, it may not model the extreme events accurately; on the contrary, if the threshold is too high, the number of remained samples may not be enough. Therefore, diagnostics for the selected threshold are necessary, but sometimes the decision is still ambiguous. It really depends on the analyzed data to decide which method to use. In this paper, we use Block Maxima as the analysis method, and the Gumbel (Max) as the fitting distribution.

The Gumbel distribution can model both maximum and minimum cases, that have different plots of probability density functions. In order to compute the estimation of WCRT, the maximum case is more adaptive. As shown in [18], the Gumbel Max distribution usually has a bounded lower tail and an unbounded upper tail ( i.e. the peak is skewed towards the lower side). From the Cumulative Density Function (CDF) F(x) = e -e -(x-μ)/β , we can get the percent point function (i.e. the inverse function of CDF):
div.formula: Est = μ -β • ln(-ln((1 -p t ) N pb ))(1)
div.p: where Est is the estimation of the upper bound at the targeted exceedence probability p t , μ and β are the best-fit location parameter (which determines the location of a distribution) and scale parameter (which relates to the spreading degree of a distribution) respectively, and N pb denotes the block size.

div.head: B. Mean, Median and Standard Deviation
div.p: In order to achieve a more efficient analysis, in this paper we present a sample filtering algorithm, which is used to create a new data set based on the original samples. In this algorithm, we need to use the mean value, the median value and the standard deviation of the analyzed data set.
Mean and median are two different ways to present the center of a data set. A mean is usually used to describe the 'average value' of a data set, which can be computed by:
div.formula: x = 1 n ∑ x i , ∀x i ∈ X (2)
div.p: where x is the mean value of the data set X with n samples. A median usually presents the 'middle value' of a data set, which can be computed by:

div.p: where M is the median value of the sorted data set X. As discussed in [21], if a distribution is symmetric, the mean and median will be exactly the same. In an asymmetric distribution with a long tail on one side, the mean will locate much closer to the tail rather than the median. In other words, the median usually represents the major samples of a data set, but the mean can be influenced a lot by a minority of farther out samples.

div.head: III. EVT-BASED WORST-CASE RESPONSE TIME ANALYSIS
A. System Model
div.p: As mentioned above, our approach provides a system independent analysis, where the analyzed system is considered as a black box. In other words, there are no specific assumptions made with respect to the target system. However, statistical analysis completely depends on the available samples. Therefore, before implementing the analysis, the analyzer has to make sure that the quality of data is approved. For example, if the samples are extracted from a simulator, the analyzer needs to guarantee that the simulator behaves really close to the real system.

In the analyzed system, there can be different types of tasks, including periodic, sporadic and even aperiodic tasks. We do not have any assumptions on the task models. However, for the convenience of making comparisons with other analysis methods in Section IV, in this paper, we only measure the estimated WCRTs of periodic tasks with the following model. A periodic task τ i can be characterized as
div.formula: τ i = (C i , T i , D i , J i , P i ).
div.p: C i is the WCET for a system execution. T i and D i denote the period and arbitrary relative deadline respectively. The release jitter J i is the time deviation between the arrival and the release of a task. P i denotes the fixed priority for each task, where the priority decreases as the value of P i increases. The analyzed system can be an operating system, a network or a distributed system. The transmission of a message in a network can be similarly modeled as the execution of a task in an operating system. Therefore, the above task model can be generally applied on messages in a network. The examples in this paper are mostly about the message transmissions since our case study is based on CAN bus communication.

We need to emphasize that the above model is just for the convenience of understanding the case studies. The analysis method presented in this paper does not depend on those detailed system or task information, since we only analyze the collected samples while keeping the analyzed system as a black box.
Moreover, the notations used in this paper have been listed in Table II.

div.head: B. WCRT Analysis 1) Sampling:
div.p: In order to satisfy the EVT requirements, we need to guarantee that the analyzed data set is formed by independent random samples with identical distribution. The population (i.e. all possible response times of the task under analysis) can be considered as a two-dimensional matrix. One dimension is based on different initial phases, which may vary for each run of the system. The other dimension is regarding all the characteristics of the system and tasks within one system run.

One important fact is that the instances of a task may influence each other within one system run as task deadlines are arbitrary. For example, when the (k + 1)th instance of task τ i arrives, the kth instance may still be occupying the shared resource (e.g. processor) due to some delay caused by the interference from other tasks. Moreover, different instances of the same task usually follow the First-Come-First-Serve (FCFS) mechanism. As a result, the dependencies can exist among some successive instances of the same task within one system run. Some declustering mechanisms can be applied to break these dependencies.

In order to analyze the collected data, we first need to convert the two-dimensional population to a one-dimensional data set. This step involves the Block Maxima selection, where we form a new data set containing the maximum response time within each system run. In this new data set, each sample is from an isolated system run, therefore, we can guarantee that i.i.d. is still satisfied. This process is presented in Algorithm 1.

Deciding the amount of sample set is an interesting and challenging issue. As we know, the larger the sample set is, the more representative it will be. However, in reality, collecting a huge number of samples may not be feasible as it requires too much simulation time. In [22], the author has discussed some suggested sample size decisions based on different factors of the statistical problem under analysis. These factors include the Margin Of Errors (MOE), the Confidence Level (CL), the degree of variability and the estimate of the whole population. Due to the difficulty of determining the accurate factor value, in this paper we use some suggested values from the references. As shown in our case studies, these suggested factor values work quite well. Hopefully, it may be easier for industrial system designers to decide specific accurate parameters based on their experience. Table I gives some of the suggested sample sizes, more details on how to estimate a sample size can also be found in [18].

As discussed above, the original population can be considered as a two-dimensional matrix. We need to consider the sample size selection on each dimension separately. For example, if we want to keep 99% confidence level on each dimension, with the above suggested factor values, the total required sample size is at least 664×664. However, sometimes the sample set based on the suggested sample sizes is not sufficient for our method due to the sample filtering process (discussed in next subsection). Therefore, we use the suggested values as the initializing sample sizes, and do some heuristic re-sampling process during the analysis if necessary. div.p: 2) Sample filtering: As shown in [19], the probability distribution of the response time of a task may include multiple peaks. Even though after the sampling step the new data set consists of maximum response time for each run, the probability distribution may still contain more than one peak (i.e. the first plot in Figure 1). It is very difficult to analyze this kind of distribution which cannot be fitted to the known distributions involved in EVT.

In [17] and [19], the authors iteratively implement a Block Maxima selection process with incremental block sizes, which can somehow transform the sample distribution to a single peak distribution. However, their solutions are based on the assumption that each system run is identical (i.e. the initial phase of each experiment does not change), which is not sufficient in general. After some tests, we notice that using their solution, the created new sample set may still fail to match the Gumbel Max distribution. For example, as shown in Figure 1.a, assume that the sample distribution includes two peaks. It is possible that in each Block Maxima selection process, the samples within the same peak are unfortunately assigned to the same block, as a result, the number of samples from both peaks are reduced at the same time. In a worse case, even if the number of blocks is reduced to the suggested lower bound 30 [17], there are still some samples located in the left peak. In this case, the sample distribution may either fail to match any continuous distribution, or match the Gumbel Min distribution instead of the Gumbel Max distribution due to the unexpected lower tail. Therefore, we propose a sample filtering algorithm (Algorithm 2) to generate a sub-data set based on the original samples, where the new sample set can be more easily fitted to the Gumbel Max distribution after the block maxima process. The main idea of this algorithm is to create a new data set by removing samples lower than a threshold. If the sample size is large enough, the collected sample set is representative at a specific confidence level p. Assume that the original data set (after the first block maxima process) is S(x) ((i.e. SampleSet BM in Algorithm 1)), then the newly created data set is S (x) = (x|x ≥ threshold, ∀x ∈ S(x)). WCRT is an upper bound of the response times which obviously must be larger than the above threshold. Therefore, WCRT is included in the distribution of S (x) at the confidence level p. Finally, after applying the block maxima process on this sub data set, the remaining samples are easier to fit the Gumbel Max distribution. As shown in Figure 2 and Figure 3, as the sample size changes, the shape of a probability distribution does not vary much. We also use a Quantile-Quantile (Q-Q) plot to graphically compare the probability distributions of data sets regarding the same message flow but with different sample sizes. As shown in Figure 4, after some point of the quantiles, the two distributions fit each other quite well. Therefore, if the analysis is based on the samples over that threshold (i.e. samples within the circles in Figure 4), we will have much more freedom on the sample size selection than analyzing the whole maxima data set. In other words, it may be much safer to analyze the samples over the threshold when it is difficult to prove the exact required sample size. The dot lines in Figure 2 and Figure 3 are the thresholds computed in our algorithm, which are obviously very close to the convergence thresholds shown in Figure 4. As we mentioned above, one primary reason of mismatching the Gumbel Max distribution is that the distribution of the remaining samples may have a much longer lower tail than the upper tail. This problem usually occurs when the distribution of the parent data set already has a quite long lower tail, or includes broad-ranged multiple peaks. In this case, it is difficult to eliminate the extremely lower samples by the block maxima process when the sample size is not huge enough. Therefore, in the newly created data set, we aim to filter out the samples located in the farther lower tail. In Moore [21], the authors have discussed that a farther out sample of a distribution will influence the mean much more than the median. In other words, a longer lower tail may result in that the mean value is much smaller than the median value of a distribution. According to this property, the aim of this sample filtering process can be converted to achieve that the mean value of the sub sample set is greater than or equal to its median value. As shown in Algorithm 2 line 3-7, the samples, which are negatively farther out from the mean value than the standard deviation, are removed from the sample set. In this filtering process, the peak of the distribution will move towards left gradually. In other words, we try to filter out the samples with lower values, so that the median will be decreased until it is lower or equal to the mean. If the remaining samples are not sufficient to support the later processes (i.e. less than the lower bound of analyzed sample sizes N lb ), we need to start a re-sample process (Algorithm 2 line 8-20). We need to confess that this sample filtering process cannot guarantee the success in the final distribution fitness process. However, according to our experiments, it can obviously increase the probability of passing the Goodness Of Fit (GOF) hypothesis test (which is usually used to test the fitness of a set of observations regarding a certain distribution).

Due to the filtering process, we have divided the parent sample set into two parts, one part contains all the samples which can exceed the threshold (i.e. can pass the sample filtering process) and the other part includes all the samples with lower values than the threshold. As discussed in Section III-B1, the samples in the parent data set SampleSet BM can be guaran-teed to be independent identically distributed. In the sample filtering process, we cut the distribution of the parent data set with respect of a given threshold, where we have taken all the samples in SampleSet BM into account. Therefore, the sample in the newly created sample set are still independent from each other, and follow a distribution which has the same shape (but proportionally enlarged) to the upper part of the parent distribution regarding the threshold. We need to emphasize that the later block maxima process is applied on the sub data set (SampleSet F = (x|x ≥ threshold, ∀x ∈ SampleSet BM )), which is created by the sample filtering process, but not on the parent data set. This condition needs to be taken into account while deriving the final exceedance probability.

div.head: C. Applicability Discussion
div.p: As we introduced above, this EVT-based WCRT analysis is system independent, which means that it can be generally ap-plied on different system models even with partial unavailable system information. This is the key benifit of this approach. However, we have to confess that comparing to the traditional RTA, this statistical method may incur more overhead due to the efforts on the sample collection process. Therefore, we consider this approach as a complement of the classic RTA but not a replacement. In other words, this EVT-based method can be utilized on the scenarios where the classic RTA is infeasible. Moreover, considering the overhead, it may not be efficient enough to apply this method during the early designing phase of the development of a system, where designers may usually need to iteratively modify system configurations. Alternatively, in the validation and evaluation phase of a system development process, our EVT-based approach may be more adaptive. In this phase, the analyzed system may have become quite complex due to the integration of a number of variant components. The complexity and unpredictability may dramatically reduce the applicability of the classic RTA.

div.head: IV. EVALUATION
div.p: In order to evaluate our EVT-based WCRT analysis method, we have applied the approach on the computation of message transmission delays over a CAN bus. In this section, we will present two case studies with different system features. A CAN bus simulator is programmed, which is used to generate data samples. In this simulator, different types of randomness that may affect the response times of messages are considered, such as processing delay, release jitter, bit stuffing percentage, physical interference, and so on. The fixed priority based scheduling mechanism is assumed together with nonpreemptive behavior. Moreover, some comparisons between our approach and the static RTA are observed according to the experimental results. In this section, the compared static RTA is based on the work in [5] and [6].

div.head: A. Case study 1
div.p: The analyzed network contains a CAN-bus with four ECUs. In the first case study, there are five periodic message flows in this network, and the utilization is around 86.28%. In this studied case, the randomness only includes stuffingbit percentage (uniformly distributed within [50%, 100%]). Therefore, the predictability of timing behavior is relatively high, and the static RTA can perform quite well. The results are presented in Table IV. The first five results (i.e. F 1 -F 5 ) are derived from 471 × 471 samples, and the last five results (i.e. F 1 -F 5 ) are computed from 385 × 385 samples with the same message parameters. In this experiment, we also applied the method presented in [19], and F 2 and F 2 fail to match the Gumbel Max distribution which means that at least one extra re-sampling process is required.

As displayed in Figure 5, when the targeted probability p t is set to 10 -5 , the pessimism of the results using our method is between 2% and 3% which is a little bit higher than using static RTA. When we decrease p t to 10 -8 , the pessimism of our approach increases to around 6%. Generally, in this case study, these two methods perform quite closely, where the static RTA performs better than our method. Obviously, this case is far from a realistic case. We need to take variant factors of a real system into account, so that the analysis can be more applicable.

div.head: B. Case study 2
div.p: This case study uses the same network topology. The CAN bus is shared by 20 message flows generated from different ECUs, and the utilization is around 66.32%. Some of the message characters are listed in Table III. In this study case, we have added some randomness in the simulation, including bit-stuffing, processing delay and release jitter. All these factors are set to be random following some truncated distributions. Note that in our approach, these factors can have totally random values without any bound limitation. However, in order to compare with static RTA, we need to make some approximations on these factors, therefore, we set some ranges for these factors. Otherwise, the static RTA cannot even be applied for the analysis. The processing delays and release jitters are assumed to follow truncated normal distributions, and the bit-stuffing probability is assumed to follow a truncated uniform distribution. We need to emphasize that these randomness factors can be assumed to be any other distributions, since our method is independent of these detailed information. First, these 20 message flows are configured to be periodic. As shown in Figure 6, as the complexity (i.e. randomness and number of flows) of the system increases, the pessimism of our analysis increases up to around 16% with p t = 10 -5 . The static RTA is no longer predominant, where it can only occasionally perform better.

Then, we further increase the system complexity, by changing the flow sets to be mixed with both periodic and sporadic flows. Five of the above flows (F 9 , F 10 , F 12 , F 14 , and F 17 ) are configured to be sporadic, with minimum inter-arrival times the same as their previous periods. As shown in the comparison (Figure 7), when we set p t to 10 -5 , the pessimism of our approach only gains a slight change (up to around 14%), but the pessimism of static RTA goes up to 19%.

As presented before, the targeted probability p t is the probability that a random sample from our newly created data set exceeds the estimated WCRT. Obviously, the lower the p t is, the higher the estimation will be. According to the observations from our tests, when p t is set to 10 -5 , our approach can produce guaranteed results with a low level of pessimism. We will spend some more efforts on optimizing and proving the selection of p t in the future work.

Some other examples are also tested with different system configurations (i.e. message parameter sets). The changes among different parameter sets focus more on the random factors which may change the complexity of the system. The general pessimism comparison is presented in Figure 8. As shown in the figure, our solution usually includes less pessimism than the static RTA. Moreover, our approach performs relatively stable as the system complexity changes. Comparatively, for some cases, the pessimism of the static RTA increases dramatically (up to almost 70%) due to the approximations of some randomness factors. The approximation of a random factor may be very small for each message flow (e.g. a processing delay may be only several microseconds). But when the network is shared by a number of flows with different types of randomness, these tiny factors together may impact the analysis result a lot. That is why the static RTA includes too much pessimism for some complex cases.

Assume that in the above examples, some of the information is not available. For example, the processing delay is not predictable, or the existences of some flows are not known. In this case, it is almost impossible to implement static RTA which requires much more detailed system information. However, the lack of system details rarely influences our method which only depends on the samples rather than static information. As a price, our analysis require some efforts on properly collecting samples and guaranteeing the quality of analyzed data.

div.head: C. PCA evaluation
div.p: In order to further figure out how different factors may incur pessimism in the results, we apply a Principal Component Analysis (PCA) [23] on our results. PCA is a widely used statistical tool to analyze the possible correlations among a set of variables. In a complex data set such as our results data, it is difficult to interpret the relations directly from the data. PCA can help us to find out which variables contribute most to the change of a response variable (i.e. which variables are the most correlated to the response variable). In a PCA loading plot (e.g. Figure 9), each variable is represented by a vector which starts from the center of the plot. The correlation of two variables can be observed from the angle (0 • -180 • ) between the corresponding vectors, as well as the length of vectors. If the angle is close to 90 • , the correlation of these two variables will be very weak (e.g. P i and Pess(EST )). As the angle decreases from 90 • towards 0 • , a positive correlation (i.e. the increase of one variable may be usually accompanied with the increase of the other variable) becomes stronger and stronger. On the contrary, as the angle increases from 90 • towards 180 • , a negative correlation becomes stronger and stronger. Moreover, if the length of a vector is too short (i.e. too close to the center), we should not derive any conclusion regarding it because this variable cannot be interpreted by the principle components.

We implement the PCA using MATLAB, and the data is normalized using zscore function. Our PCA procedure takes into account different message characteristics mentioned in Section III, where a message is considered as a task. In this model of network communications, C i denotes message transmission latency without interferences. U task represents the utilization of a task (i.e. a message) which can be simply computed as C i T i . As shown in Figure 9, the pessimism of the results of our method has a very weak correlation with P i which is however strongly correlated to the pessimism of the static RTA. A message flow with a lower priority may get more interference comparing to messages with higher priorities. Therefore, using the static RTA, more interference can result in more pessimism due to the pessimism involved in each interference calculation step. That illustrates our previous observation that when we increase the number of flows in the network, the pessimism of the static RTA obviously increases, but our method performs relatively stable. Moreover, C i and J i are correlated with the pessimism of both methods at the same level but with opposite effects. Due to the design of our simulator, the higher C i (or J i ) is, the more variation it may have. In other words, a higher C i (or J i ) may incur more random behaviors, as a result, the corresponding approximation in the static RTA may include more pessimism. On the contrary, as the randomness of the samples increases, we may get more variational samples which can result in a more accurate fit of distribution in our analysis. Therefore, as shown in the figure, C i and J i are positively correlated to the pessimism of the static RTA, and negatively correlated to the pessimism of our method. This is consistent with our observations in the previous evaluation phase.

div.head: V. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORKS
div.p: In this paper, we present an Extreme Value Theory based statistical method to estimate worst case response times of complex real-time systems. Our solution is an extension and optimization of the work in [17] and [19]. In order to evaluate the performance of our method, we apply the analysis on Controller Area Networks communications. As shown in our results, comparing to static RTA, our approach usually performs more stable and produces less pessimism when the complexity of the system increases. Moreover, our approach does not depend on detailed system information, which means it can be applied on different types of systems or even systems with unknown information.

As we discussed, for statistical methods, the more samples collected, the more accurate the results are. However, collecting more samples will definitely increase the overhead of the analysis, and it is difficult to prove what the exact sufficient sample size is. In this paper, we use suggested values from some statistical references which perform well according to our evaluation. It will be useful to investigate that threshold, so that we can decrease the sample size while keeping the same performance. Moreover, the evaluation of our method depends on the credibility of the best practice simulation. We can further apply PCA on the analyzed system. Based on the observations, some stress testing can be implemented, which can provide us more trustable evaluations.
